summary: Defines three mechanisms for getting a URI that points to a user's calendar and free or busy times, for use with vCard and LDAP. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: When you want to arrange a meeting with someone, you need to know when they are busy and where to send the invitation. This document defines four kinds of web address for that, and says how to put them into a business card file or a company directory.

questions: how to find a persons calendar in ldap
how to find free busy time with ldap
subtitle: Four kinds of web address for a person's calendar, and how to publish them in a vCard or a directory.

tldr.problem: To arrange a meeting you need to know when the other person is busy and where to send the invitation. There was no standard way for a user to publish those addresses, so every client and directory invented its own.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines four classes of URI: one for busy time data, one for live access to the calendar, one for a published snapshot of the calendar, and one for where meeting requests should be sent. It then adds the matching vCard properties and LDAP attributes for carrying them.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2739 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 6350, which replaced the vCard 3.0 format it was written against.

today: RFC 2739 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It was later updated by RFC 6350, which defines the current vCard format and replaced the vCard 3.0 format that this document was written against, so the two should be read together.

sections.title: Locating Someone's Calendar
sections.content:
The memo defines four classes of URIs, because URIs are more useful if it is understood what they point to. A calendaring and scheduling client is referred to in the document as a CUA.

These four URIs provide valuable pointers to calendaring and scheduling data that other users need in order to know when to schedule meetings. The document then sets out several possibilities for how users can communicate these URIs to other users, covering manual transfer, personal data exchange using a vCard, and directory lookup using the LDAP protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of the document is simple: give people a standard way to say where their calendar is, so that other people's software can find it without guessing.

sections.title: The Four URI Classes
sections.content:
The free/busy URI, FBURL, is a transport-independent location where a client can obtain information about when a user is busy. At the present time it points only to busy time data, and future revisions may provide for the extended capability of publishing free time data. If a client retrieved the data using FTP or HTTP it would get back an iCalendar object containing one or more VFREEBUSY calendar components, and if a MIME transport is used the response is contained within a text/calendar body part. The amount of busy time data will generally be pre-determined, for example one month, and as a guideline it is recommended that the previous six weeks of busy time data be published at the location associated with the FBURL. If the URI points to a file resource, it is recommended that the file extension be ifb.

The Calendar Access URI, CAPURI, is a protocol-independent location from which a client can communicate with a user's entire calendar. The semantics for using this URI as an access protocol locator are yet to be defined by the IETF CALSCH Working Group, and were to be addressed in a Calendar Access Protocol specification.

The Calendar URI, CALURI, is a protocol-independent location from which a client can retrieve an entire copy of a user's calendar, obtaining a published snapshot of the user's calendar. If the URI is an HTTP URI, the content returned with a GET should be a text/calendar body part containing one or more iCalendar objects. If it is an FTP URI, the resource should be a file with an ics file extension containing one or more iCalendar objects.

There are many cases where a user may have more than one calendar. To make the case of multiple calendars simpler for clients, the concept of the default calendar is introduced: one that the user has designated as the calendar other users should look at when accessing the user's calendar or retrieving the user's free/busy time. The default calendar may in fact include rolled-up information from all the user's other calendars, which may only exist for organizational purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: One address says when you are busy, one is a snapshot of your whole calendar, one is a live connection to your calendar, and one says where invitations should be sent. A user may have several calendars, so one of them is marked as the default.

sections.title: How the Addresses Are Distributed
sections.content:
The simplest way to obtain these URIs is for a user to communicate them using some out-of-band mechanism, such as verbally, in an e-mail message, or by printing the URIs on a paper business card. The user then enters them into their calendaring software manually.

A more sophisticated way is for users to publish vCards containing these URIs. The vCard object can be transferred between one another, and since many e-mail clients allow a user to include a vCard automatically with every message, this provides a simple, transparent way to distribute the calendaring URIs. On the receiving end, an e-mail client with an integrated vCard database can provide a way to look up calendaring URIs for users whose vCards are stored locally.

Another way is to look them up in a directory using the LDAP protocol. If a user's URIs can be found by directory lookup, they should in general be considered more up-to-date than URIs in any vCards that are stored locally.
sections.plainLanguage: You can write the addresses down, attach them to your email as a business card, or let people look them up in the company directory. A directory lookup is normally the freshest, because a stored card can be out of date.

sections.title: The vCard Properties
sections.content:
Since the vCard specification does not say how to encode calendaring URIs in a vCard, this section is an extension that specifies how to encode them. Inside a vCard object four new properties are defined: CALURI, CAPURI, CALADRURI and FBURL. Any vCard can have one or more of these properties, each representing a calendar or free/busy time associated with the user. One of these properties can be designated as the default by adding the PREF parameter.

The registrations say what each property is for. FBURL specifies the URI for a user's busy time, and where multiple FBURL properties are specified the default is indicated with the PREF parameter; if the iCalendar object is represented as a file its file type should be ifb. CALADRURI specifies the location to which an event request should be sent for the user. CAPURI specifies a protocol-independent location from which a client can communicate with a user's entire calendar. CALURI specifies the URI for a user's calendar, and the property should contain a URI pointing to an iCalendar object associated with a snapshot of the user's calendar store, with a file type of ics.
sections.plainLanguage: The business card format gets four new fields, one for each kind of address. The card can hold several of each, and the one marked as preferred is the default.

sections.title: The LDAP Attributes
sections.content:
To encode the calendaring URIs in the directory, one object class and eight attributes are defined. The object class is calEntry, derived from TOP, which contains the four calendaring attributes. The attributes are calCalURI, calFBURL, calCAPURI, calCalAdrURI, calOtherCalURIs, calOtherFBURLs, calOtherCAPURIs and calOtherCalAdrURIs.

The calCalURI contains the URI to a snapshot of the user's entire default calendar, calFBURL contains the URI to the user's default busy time data, calCAPURI contains a URI that can be used to communicate with the user's calendar, and calCalAdrURI contains a URI that points to the location to which event requests should be sent for that user. The four calOther attributes are multi-valued properties: calOtherCalURIs holds URIs to snapshots of other calendars the user may have, calOtherFBURLs holds URIs to other free/busy data, calOtherCAPURIs holds URIs to other calendars, and calOtherCalAdrURIs holds URIs to other locations to which the user may want event requests sent. There is no predetermined order to the values in either multi-valued property.

All eight attributes have the syntax IA5String and use caseIgnoreMatch for equality and substring matching. The object class identifier is 1.2.840.113556.1.5.87, and the attribute identifiers run from 1.2.840.113556.1.4.478 for calCalURI to 1.2.840.113556.1.4.485 for calOtherCalAdrURIs.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory gets one new kind of entry and eight new fields. Four hold the default addresses and four hold any extra ones, and each of the extra ones can hold several addresses with no particular order.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Standard vCard and LDAP security rules and support apply for the extensions described in this document, and there are no special security issues for these extensions.

LDAP servers may permit anonymous clients to refresh entries which they did not create. Servers are also permitted to control refresh access to an entry by requiring clients to bind before issuing a RefreshRequest, which has implications for server performance and scalability.

vCard objects may have been created by an entity other than that represented by the vCard, so recipients should be certain of the source that generated the vCard. Care should also be taken in making use of information obtained from directory servers that has been supplied by the client, as it may now be out of date. In many networks, for example, IP addresses are automatically assigned when a host connects to the network and may be reassigned if that host later disconnects, so an IP address obtained from the directory may no longer be assigned to the host that placed the address there.
sections.plainLanguage: The addresses themselves are ordinary web addresses and carry the usual risks. Two things are worth remembering: a business card may have been written by somebody other than the person it describes, and a directory entry may still point at an address that has since been given to a different machine.

data.title: Example vCard
data.code:
BEGIN:VCARD
VERSION:3.0
N:Dun;Alec
FN:Alec Dun
EMAIL;INTERNET:user@host1.com
CALADRURI;PREF:mailto:user@host1.com
CALURI;PREF:http://cal.host1.com/user/cal.ics
FBURL;PREF:http://cal.host1.com/user/fb.ifb
CALURI:http://cal.company.com/projectA/pjtA.ics
FBURL:http://cal.company.com/projectA/pjtAfb.ifb
END:VCARD
